plants.fl_notes: Ready in about a month: a good first crop for kids.
Very cold tolerant and keeps producing all winter.
Grow in loose, deep soil or a raised bed so roots come out straight.
A cool-season herb here: it bolts fast once nights warm up in spring.
Hates wet feet: plant high in sandy soil or in a pot, and water sparingly.
Always grow mint in a pot: in the ground it spreads everywhere.
Loves Florida heat and takes some neglect. Bring pots in on cold nights.
A heat lover that grows into a big clump. Cut stalks at the base as needed.
Pick low-chill southern highbush varieties and plant two or more for better crops. Needs acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5): plant in pine bark.
'Celeste' and 'Brown Turkey' do well here. Mulch thickly: figs have shallow roots and nematodes are common in sand.
A Florida native grape that shrugs off the diseases that kill bunch grapes here. Needs a sturdy trellis.
Citrus greening (HLB) is widespread in Florida: buy only from a registered nursery with a certified tree, and don't move citrus plants between counties.
The most cold-hardy citrus, the best pick for north and central Florida. Buy a certified tree from a registered nursery (citrus greening).
South Florida only in the ground. Pick a compact variety; young trees need cover below 32°F.
Thirsty and hungry, and leaves shred in wind. Freezes back below 28°F but usually regrows.
Fruits in under a year. Needs fast-draining soil: standing water after storms kills it.
Only low-chill varieties from UF/IFAS ('UFSun', 'Gulfking') fruit this far south.
Pick thornless varieties bred for the South and give them a simple wire trellis.
Plant the leafy top of a store-bought pineapple. Fun, tough, and fine in a pot.
Pick a cold-hardy variety (e.g. 'Brogdon', 'Lila'). Laurel wilt is spreading in Florida; ask your Extension office before planting.
FISC Category I invasive: birds spread the seeds into natural areas. Never suggested.
Own-root shrub roses like Knock Out are the easiest in Florida. Water at the base in the morning to limit black spot.
An old garden tea rose that thrives in Florida heat. For hybrid teas, buy plants grafted on 'Fortuniana' rootstock, which handles sandy soil and nematodes.
The 'Florida cracker rose': an heirloom found in old Florida gardens, tough and almost always in bloom.
Sow seeds in spring: easy cut flowers that butterflies love. Profusion types resist mildew.
Kids love them: seeds sprout in days and plants pass their heads in a month.
Blooms almost all year in central and south Florida, a butterfly magnet. Red ones draw the most butterflies.
Plant the crown slightly above the soil so it doesn't rot in summer rains. Great cut flowers.
Cheap, cheerful edging for vegetable beds. Plant in spring and fall; summer heat wears them out.
Colorful leaves for shade, grown from tubers (most come from Lake Placid, FL). Leaves die back in winter and return in spring. Tubers survive winter in the ground in central and south Florida.
Tough tropical color for shade. Flush the water cups weekly in summer so mosquitoes can't breed.
Rare true-blue flowers most of the year. Drought tolerant once established.
Thirsty: wilts every hot afternoon in full sun. Needs morning sun and afternoon shade; acidic soil turns flowers blue.
Nearly indestructible clumps for low-care beds. Not native, but not invasive.
